**For teachers only. Do not share with students.**

This document runs the whole practical from the raw data and answers
every question of `rresearch_tutorial.Rmd`, including the homework.
Knit it in the `yeast_project` folder (with `data/yeast_cds.fa.gz` and
`data/yeast_genome.fa.gz`) in RStudio, after the `yeast-tools` Conda
environment with SeqKit has been created. All numbers below come from
Ensembl R64-1-1 (*S. cerevisiae*), the files the students download.

```{r setup, message=FALSE}
library(tidyverse)
library(ggrepel)
# Same line as in the student notebook: lets bash chunks find seqkit
Sys.setenv(PATH = paste(path.expand("~/.conda/envs/yeast-tools/bin"),
                        Sys.getenv("PATH"), sep = ":"))
dir.create("results", showWarnings = FALSE)
```

# Exercise 1: Inspect the sequences

> How many sequence records are there? Why would counting all the lines
> give a different answer?

```{bash}
# Records: one header line (starting with >) per sequence
zcat data/yeast_cds.fa.gz | grep -c '^>'
# All lines: headers + sequence lines (each sequence is wrapped over many lines)
zcat data/yeast_cds.fa.gz | wc -l
```

**Answer.** 6,600 records. Counting all lines gives 155,818, because the
sequence of each record is spread over many lines; only the header
starts with `>`.

*Common mistake:* `grep -c '>'` without `^` gives the same number here,
but would also count a `>` anywhere in a line.

# Exercise 2: Process the sequences with SeqKit

`-a` adds extra columns (quartiles, N50, GC) to the standard summary;
the students run it without `-a`, which already gives min, average and
max length.

```{bash}
seqkit stats -a data/yeast_cds.fa.gz data/yeast_genome.fa.gz 2>/dev/null
```

The gene table, exactly as in the tutorial:

```{bash}
zcat data/yeast_cds.fa.gz | grep '>' > results/cds_headers.txt
cut -d ' ' -f 1,3 results/cds_headers.txt | sed -e 's/>//' -e 's/_mRNA//' -e 's/chromosome:R64-1-1://' -e 's/[ :]/\t/g' > results/positions.tsv
seqkit fx2tab -n -i -l data/yeast_cds.fa.gz > results/lengths.tsv
printf 'record_id\tchromosome\tstart\tend\tstrand\tlength_bp\n' > results/yeast_cds.tsv
paste results/positions.tsv results/lengths.tsv | cut -f 1-5,7 >> results/yeast_cds.tsv
head -n 3 results/yeast_cds.tsv
```

The same table with SeqKit only, and a check that both are identical:

```{bash}
printf 'record_id\tchromosome\tstart\tend\tstrand\tlength_bp\n' > results/yeast_cds_seqkit.tsv
seqkit replace -p '_mRNA cds chromosome:R64-1-1:(\S+) .*' -r ' $1' data/yeast_cds.fa.gz | seqkit fx2tab -n -l | tr ' :' '\t\t' >> results/yeast_cds_seqkit.tsv
diff results/yeast_cds.tsv results/yeast_cds_seqkit.tsv && echo "Both tables are the same"
```

The chromosome table:

```{bash}
printf 'chromosome\tchromosome_bp\n' > results/chromosomes.tsv
zcat data/yeast_genome.fa.gz | grep '>' | cut -d ':' -f 4,6 | sed 's/:/\t/' >> results/chromosomes.tsv
cat results/chromosomes.tsv
```

Header lengths next to the lengths counted by SeqKit. `diff` prints
nothing if they agree:

```{bash}
tail -n +2 results/chromosomes.tsv > results/header_lengths.tsv
seqkit fx2tab -n -i -l data/yeast_genome.fa.gz | diff results/header_lengths.tsv - && echo "Header lengths agree with SeqKit"
```

> How many genes and how many chromosomes are there? What are the
> shortest, longest and average CDS lengths? One "chromosome" is called
> `Mito`: what is it?

**Answer.** 6,600 genes (protein-coding CDS) on 17 sequences: 16 nuclear
chromosomes (I–XVI) and `Mito`. CDS length: shortest 51 bp, longest
14,733 bp, average 1,327.6 bp. `Mito` is the **mitochondrial genome**
(85,779 bp, 28 CDS), a separate small circular genome inside the
mitochondria.

> Do the chromosome lengths in the headers agree with the lengths counted
> by SeqKit? Why is it worth checking?

**Answer.** Yes, all 17 agree. A header is just text written by someone;
the sequence is the actual data. Checking catches truncated or corrupted
downloads, edited or wrong headers, or a mix-up between genome versions.
General lesson: verify metadata against the data whenever it is cheap.

# Exercise 3: Genes and chromosomes in R

```{r}
genes <- read_tsv("results/yeast_cds.tsv", show_col_types = FALSE)
nrow(genes)   # 6,600: same as the record count in Exercise 1

genes_summary <- genes %>%
  summarise(genes = n(),
            mean_length = mean(length_bp),
            median_length = median(length_bp))
genes_summary
write_tsv(genes_summary, "results/summary.tsv")

chromosomes <- read_tsv("results/chromosomes.tsv", show_col_types = FALSE) %>%
  left_join(count(genes, chromosome, name = "genes"), by = "chromosome") %>%
  mutate(genes_per_100kb = genes / chromosome_bp * 100000)
write_tsv(chromosomes, "results/chromosomes_genes.tsv")
```

> Are mean and median CDS length similar? What could explain a
> difference?

```{r}
summary(genes$length_bp)
```

**Answer.** Mean 1,328 bp, median 1,062 bp. The distribution is skewed
to the right (see the histogram in Exercise 5): a few very long genes
pull the mean up, while the median is robust to them.

> For most genes, `end - start + 1` equals `length_bp`, but not for all.
> Use `filter()` to find the genes where they differ. How many are there,
> and why is the gene longer on the chromosome than its CDS?

```{r}
spliced <- genes %>%
  filter(end - start + 1 != length_bp) %>%
  mutate(intron_bp = end - start + 1 - length_bp)   # extra length on the chromosome
nrow(spliced)
count(spliced, nuclear = chromosome != "Mito")
spliced %>% arrange(desc(intron_bp)) %>% head()
```

**Answer.** 287 genes. The CDS contains only the coding exons; the
chromosome coordinates span the whole gene, including the **introns**
that are spliced out. 276 are nuclear genes (only ~5% of yeast genes
have introns, usually one short one) and 11 are mitochondrial; the
largest differences are mitochondrial genes such as COX1 (Q0045), which
has many long introns. `end - start + 1` is never smaller than
`length_bp`.

> Which chromosome has the most genes? Is it also the longest? Which
> chromosome has the highest and which the lowest gene density?

```{r}
chromosomes %>% arrange(desc(genes))
chromosomes %>% arrange(desc(genes_per_100kb))
```

**Answer.** Chromosome IV has the most genes (836) and is also the
longest (1.53 Mb). Highest density: III (58.1 genes per 100 kb). Lowest:
`Mito` (32.6); among the nuclear chromosomes, I (50.8). The nuclear
chromosomes are all very similar (51–58 per 100 kb).

> Change the example above to list the genes on `Mito`, from longest to
> shortest.

```{r}
genes %>%
  filter(chromosome == "Mito") %>%
  arrange(desc(length_bp))
```

**Answer.** 28 genes; the longest is Q0055 (2,565 bp). Note several
genes share the start 13818: these are COX1 and the intron-encoded ORFs
(AI1–AI5) that start in COX1 exons.

# Exercise 4: Strands, gaps and overlaps

```{r}
count(genes, strand)

neighbours <- genes %>%
  arrange(chromosome, start) %>%
  group_by(chromosome) %>%
  mutate(left_neighbour = lag(record_id),   # added for the homework
         gap_bp = start - lag(end) - 1,
         orientation = case_when(lag(strand) == strand ~ "tandem",
                                 lag(strand) == -1 ~ "divergent",
                                 lag(strand) == 1 ~ "convergent")) %>%
  ungroup() %>%
  filter(!is.na(gap_bp))

orientation_summary <- neighbours %>%
  group_by(orientation) %>%
  summarise(pairs = n(),
            median_gap = median(gap_bp),
            overlapping = sum(gap_bp < 0))
orientation_summary
write_tsv(orientation_summary, "results/orientations.tsv")
sum(neighbours$gap_bp < 0)
```

> Are genes spread evenly over the two strands?

**Answer.** Yes, almost evenly: 3,331 on the + strand, 3,269 on the −
strand (50.5% vs 49.5%).

> How many neighbouring genes overlap in total? Are overlapping genes
> mostly on the same strand or on opposite strands?

**Answer.** 646 pairs overlap. Most are on opposite strands
(229 convergent + 302 divergent = 531); only 115 tandem pairs (same
strand) overlap. Many overlaps are small ORFs (e.g. dubious ORFs, `-A`
and `-B` genes) inside or across a larger gene.

> Which orientation has the longest gaps and which the shortest? Use the
> second scheme to explain why.

**Answer.** Shortest: convergent (median 206 bp). Longest: tandem
(380 bp) and divergent (379 bp), about the same here, because divergent
pairs overlap most often (302 negative gaps) and that pulls their median
down. Without overlaps divergent is clearly longest (Exercise 5). A convergent gap holds
only the two 3′ ends (terminators), no promoter. A tandem gap holds the
promoter of one gene, and a divergent gap holds the promoters of both
genes (often a shared bidirectional promoter), so they need more space.
*Accept "divergent" as the longest, as long as the explanation uses
promoters.*

# Exercise 5: Make figures with ggplot2

```{r}
p_length <- ggplot(genes, aes(x = length_bp)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 40, fill = "steelblue", colour = "white") +
  labs(x = "CDS length (bp)", y = "Number of genes") +
  theme_minimal()
p_length

p_chrom <- ggplot(chromosomes, aes(x = chromosome_bp / 1000000, y = genes,
                                   label = chromosome)) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_text_repel() +
  labs(x = "Chromosome length (Mb)", y = "Number of genes") +
  theme_minimal()
p_chrom

p_gaps <- ggplot(neighbours, aes(x = gap_bp)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 50, fill = "steelblue", colour = "white") +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0, colour = "red") +
  coord_cartesian(xlim = c(-1000, 3000)) +
  labs(x = "Gap between neighbouring genes (bp)", y = "Number of gene pairs") +
  theme_minimal()
p_gaps

p_orient <- ggplot(filter(neighbours, gap_bp > 0),
                   aes(x = orientation, y = gap_bp, fill = orientation)) +
  geom_boxplot(outlier.alpha = 0.2) +
  scale_y_log10() +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Gap between neighbouring genes (bp)") +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(legend.position = "none")
p_orient
```

> What relationship do you see between chromosome length and number of
> genes? Roughly how many genes are there per 100 kb? Which point does
> not follow the pattern, and why might that be?

```{r}
# Slope of the line through the nuclear chromosomes, as genes per 100 kb
fit <- lm(genes ~ chromosome_bp, data = filter(chromosomes, chromosome != "Mito"))
coef(fit)["chromosome_bp"] * 100000
# Overall density
sum(chromosomes$genes) / sum(chromosomes$chromosome_bp) * 100000
```

**Answer.** An almost perfectly linear relationship: longer chromosomes
have proportionally more genes, about 54 genes per 100 kb (one gene
every ~1.8 kb). `Mito` lies below the line (32.6 per 100 kb): the
mitochondrial genome is a separate genome with its own organisation,
long introns, rRNA/tRNA genes (not in the CDS file) and long AT-rich
non-coding regions. (Students may say "it is too small to see" - point
them to the density table.)

> Make a bar plot of the gene density of each chromosome with
> `geom_col()` (x = `chromosome`, y = `genes_per_100kb`), and save it
> under a different file name.

```{r}
p_density <- ggplot(chromosomes, aes(x = chromosome, y = genes_per_100kb)) +
  geom_col(fill = "steelblue") +
  labs(x = "Chromosome", y = "Genes per 100 kb") +
  theme_minimal()
p_density
ggsave("results/gene_density.png", p_density, width = 8, height = 5)
```

*Optional improvement:* chromosomes are sorted alphabetically
(I, II, III, IV, IX, ...). `aes(x = factor(chromosome, levels = chromosomes$chromosome), ...)`
keeps the file order.

> What is the most common gap size? Does the boxplot agree with your
> answer about orientations in Exercise 4?

```{r}
# Most common 50-bp bins of the gap histogram
neighbours %>%
  count(gap_bin = floor(gap_bp / 50) * 50) %>%
  arrange(desc(n)) %>%
  head(3)
```

**Answer.** Around 200–300 bp (the highest bar is 250–300 bp): yeast
genes are packed closely with short intergenic regions. Yes: the
convergent box is clearly lowest, divergent and tandem higher, as in
the medians from Exercise 4, and more clearly: without overlapping
pairs the order is convergent < tandem < divergent (medians below), i.e.
no promoter < one promoter < two promoters.

```{r}
neighbours %>%
  filter(gap_bp > 0) %>%
  group_by(orientation) %>%
  summarise(median_gap = median(gap_bp))
```

> The human genome is about 3,100 Mb long and has about 20,000
> protein-coding genes. Calculate its gene density in genes per 100 kb
> and compare it with yeast. What does this tell you about the human
> genome?

```{r}
human <- 20000 / 3100e6 * 100000
human
54.3 / human   # how many times denser yeast is
```

**Answer.** About 0.65 genes per 100 kb, roughly 80 times lower than
yeast (54). Only ~1–2% of the human genome codes for protein; the rest
is large introns, long intergenic regions with regulatory elements, and
repeats (transposons). Yeast has a compact genome with few, short
introns.

**Answer.** Needed: `rresearch_notebook.Rmd` (all code and text) and a

# Homework

**1. The ten longest genes.**

```{r}
longest <- genes %>%
  arrange(desc(length_bp)) %>%
  slice_head(n = 10)
longest
write_tsv(longest, "results/longest_genes.tsv")
count(longest, chromosome, sort = TRUE)
```

They are on XII (3 genes), II and IV (2 each), and XI, VIII and XV. The
longest is YLR106C (MDN1, 14,733 bp), followed by YKR054C (DYN1, the
dynein heavy chain). No pattern by chromosome: long genes are spread
over the genome.

**2. Overlapping gene pairs.**

```{r}
overlaps <- neighbours %>% filter(gap_bp < 0)
count(overlaps, orientation)

p_overlap <- ggplot(overlaps, aes(x = orientation)) +
  geom_bar(fill = "steelblue") +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Number of overlapping pairs") +
  theme_minimal()
p_overlap
ggsave("results/overlaps.png", p_overlap, width = 6, height = 5)

# Largest overlaps, with both genes of the pair
overlaps %>%
  arrange(gap_bp) %>%
  select(left_neighbour, record_id, chromosome, gap_bp, orientation) %>%
  head(10)
```

Divergent pairs overlap most often (302), then convergent (229), then
tandem (115). On SGD, most overlapping genes turn out to be poorly
characterised: many are *dubious ORFs* or small ORFs (names ending in
`-A`/`-B`, e.g. YNL339W-B, YIL177W-A in subtelomeric regions), or
intron-encoded ORFs in the mitochondrial genome. The point of the
exercise: annotation includes uncertain genes, and overlaps often
indicate them.

**3. Paragraph (example).** Yeast genes are densely packed, about 54
genes per 100 kb on all nuclear chromosomes, so gene number grows in
proportion to chromosome length; the mitochondrial genome is less
dense. Genes are spread evenly over both strands. Gaps between
neighbours are short (typically 200–300 bp): convergent pairs, which
share only terminators, have the shortest gaps, while divergent and
tandem pairs, whose gaps contain promoters, have longer ones. About 10%
of neighbouring pairs overlap, mostly on opposite strands. The human
genome is ~80 times less dense, with most DNA non-coding. A pattern in a
plot shows an association, not its cause: other variables (e.g.
centromeres, repeats, annotation quality, how genes were predicted) can
produce the same pattern, and testing a cause needs an experiment or a
model that rules out alternatives.
